title: Observation of magnetic quantum phase crossovers in a semiconductor spin ladder
authors: Elizaveta Morozova, Xin Zhang, Utso Bhattacharya, Pablo Cova Fariña, Daniel Jirovec, Alexander Nico-Katz, Stefan D. Oosterhout, Sougato Bose, Giordano Scappucci, Menno Veldhorst, Eugene Demler, Lieven M. K. Vandersypen
abstract: Understanding collective phases of strongly correlated quantum magnets relies on theoretically tractable model systems with precise microscopic control. Antiferromagnetic spin ladders provide such a setting, hosting field-tunable gapped and gapless phases at half filling and unconventional pairing tendencies upon doping. Here, we realize a programmable Heisenberg spin ladder in a half-filled germanium quantum dot array featuring site-resolved, continuously tunable exchange interactions. Under a fixed magnetic field, we vary the rung and leg coupling to map the rung-singlet, canted antiferromagnetic, and fully polarized phases. Hamiltonian-learning protocols combining equilibrium and dynamical measurements quantitatively characterize the ladder, incorporating spin-orbit interactions to reproduce the observed crossover behavior. Measurements of higher-order spin correlators -- including four-point correlations inaccessible to conventional bulk probes -- reveal signatures of the underlying phase structure despite the finite size. Our results establish germanium quantum dot arrays as a controllable platform for quantum magnetism, opening routes to investigate unconventional superconductivity in doped ladders.
summary: This experiment demonstrates the ability to engineer and observe quantum phase crossovers in an artificial spin ladder built from germanium quantum dots. By tuning the magnetic interactions, the researchers mapped out three distinct magnetic phases, confirming theoretical predictions using advanced measurements of higher-order spin correlations. This establishes quantum dot arrays as a highly controllable platform for investigating unconventional superconductivity and quantum magnetism.
main_problem: The research aims to understand the collective quantum phases and crossovers in strongly correlated quantum magnets, specifically focusing on antiferromagnetic spin ladders.
main_result: The authors successfully mapped the ground state evolution across three distinct magnetic phases (Rung-Singlet, Canted Antiferromagnetic, and Fully Polarized) by tuning exchange interactions in a semiconductor quantum dot array.
method: The study employs Hamiltonian-learning protocols combining equilibrium and dynamical measurements, utilizing higher-order spin correlators inaccessible to conventional bulk probes.
model_or_system: The physical system is a programmable Heisenberg spin ladder realized in a half-filled germanium quantum dot array. The system is modeled by an effective XXZ Heisenberg Hamiltonian derived from a Fermi-Hubbard model, allowing tuning of rung and leg couplings.
key_observables: Triplet number distribution, variance of triplet number, and four-point spin correlators ($\langle eS^+_i eS^-_{j} angle$ vs $\langle eS^z_i eS^z_j angle$).
important_parameters: Rung coupling ($J_{\perp}$), leg coupling ($J_{\parallel}$), and magnetic field ($h_z$). Key regimes include $J_{\parallel} \approx 0$ (dimer limit) and the intermediate Canted Antiferromagnetic (CAFM) phase.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of the effective spin Hamiltonian and notes that the general Hamiltonian description neglects anisotropic exchange interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device concept and the phase diagram, showing how $\langle M angle$ and $	ext{Var}(M)$ track the crossover between the RS, CAFM, and FP phases. Correlator plots confirm enhanced transverse coherence in the CAFM region.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical platform (Ge quantum dots) and the theoretical model (Heisenberg ladder Hamiltonian). It then details the experimental measurement techniques using spin-gap parameters and higher-order correlators to map the phase boundaries and characterize the crossover behavior across the three distinct magnetic phases.
why_interesting: This work provides an unprecedentedly controllable solid-state platform to study fundamental quantum magnetism, directly linking theoretical models of strongly correlated electron systems (like the Hubbard model) to measurable quantum phenomena in solid-state devices.
